pr_title: set secondary address on host-network pods
pr_body:
host-network pods IPs are obtained from the reported kubelet nodeIPs.

Historically, host-network podIPs are immutable once set, but when
we've added dual-stack support, we didn't consider that the secondary
IP address may not be present at the same time that the primary nodeIP.

If a secondary IP address is added to a node after the host-network pods
IPs are set, we can add the secondary host-network pod IP address
maintaining the current behavior of not updating the current podIPs on
host-network pods.

This is an alternative to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/105410 ,
without having to change the kubelet and host-network podIPs behavior
xref: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/pull/3000

/kind bug
```release-note
CRI-API: IPs returned by PodSandboxNetworkStatus are ignored by the kubelet for host-network pods.
```
Fixes: #105320

> we didn't consider that the secondary

why wouldn't it be? / why wouldn't we expect you to restart kubelet in that case?

> CRIO and containerd doesn't send IPs for host network pods
> ...
> but they can.

So, originally, cri-o _did_ send IPs for host network pods, and kubelet just accepted them. But this was a bad idea, because it means that if you wanted to override kubelet's `--node-ip`, then you probably _also_ had to override cri-o's idea of what the default host IP was or your host-network pods would end up with the wrong IP. Kubelet already had the fallback code to set host-network podIPs itself if the CRI didn't do it, so we just changed cri-o to leave the pod IPs blank for hostNetwork pods. (https://github.com/cri-o/cri-o/pull/2944)

I'm not sure what the historical situation with containerd was.

The unit test is testing that if the CRI _does_ set the pod IPs, that kubelet continues to behave like it did historically, so as to not break CRIs that still do that.

issue_context.title: Host Networking pods get only 1 IP address during fresh deployment or reboot of nodes in dual stack enabled cluster
issue_context.body:
**What happened:**

We have installed k8s cluster on openstack cloud provider setup. K8s cluster is dual-stack enabled.
During fresh deployment or worker node reboots (master nodes , worker nodes) , k8s control plane pods (other host networking pods aswell) such as kube-proxy, kube-scheduler , kube-controller-manager get only 1 IP address instead of dual-stack address.

**What you expected to happen:**

We expect all host networking pods to get dual-stack addresses , since cluster is dual-stack enabled.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):**
a) Openstack cloud provider setup with minimum 4-5 VMs.
b) 3 master nodes, 2 worker nodes
c) Execute simultaneous reboot of all nodes.

Environment:
Kubernetes version : v1.22.0
comments:
/sig network
/triage needs-information
/assign @khenidak 

Hi @hanamantagoudvk When you describe your node what are the IPs assigned in node object? 

kubelet copies from node object into pods. The way they are set on node object is by the cloud provider, manual via kubelet's `--node-ip` flag or auto-detect which prefers IPv4 (check: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kubelet/).

> Hi @hanamantagoudvk When you describe your node what are the IPs assigned in node object?

when i describe the node object , they contain dual-stack addresses.
 
> kubelet copies from node object into pods. The way they are set on node object is by the cloud provider, manual via kubelet's `--node-ip` flag or auto-detect which prefers IPv4 (check: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kubelet/).

Yes i debugged kubelet with few additional logs. I could see that when kubelet is reading node obj to create these static pods, it sees only 1 IP. But eventually node object is populated with both the addresses. 

I also understand, `--node-ip` is for baremetal installation. But we have cloud provider setup which might be delaying setting both the IPs in node obj. Before cloud provider sets both the IPs ,kubelet is fast enough to create these static pods.

Let me know if you need any additional logs.

thanks again @hanamantagoudvk

Few additional questions:
- are these static pods?
- When the node object gets its dualstack addresses and pods were created **after** the node object updates do you still get single address pods?

> When the node object gets its dualstack addresses and pods were created after the node object updates do you still get single address pods?

> I also understand, --node-ip is for baremetal installation. But we have cloud provider setup which might be delaying setting both the IPs in node obj. Before cloud provider sets both the IPs ,kubelet is fast enough to create these static pods.

I've chatted with the reporter in slack, it seems a race on populating the node addresses by the cloud-provider,

@aojea Yes. It would seem so. Two things here i am trying to clarify.
1. With cloud providers node register with taints (no schedule) until cloud provider adds provider-Id and other details including IPs.
2. If these are static pods then I am not sure if kubelet respects no-schedule (those are respected by scheduler which is out of the picture for static pods) If they are then they will run - most likely - before node gets IP addresses from cloud provider. 

The questions i asked above should put some lights on this.
  
 > The solution in all cases is to check IPs assigned host net pods and if they are missing one then we must add it. But let us narrow down this specific before trying anything.

> * are these static pods?

Yes i am referring to kube-proxy , kube-api-server ,kube-scheduler pods which use host-networking.

> * When the node object gets its dualstack addresses and pods were created **after** the node object updates do you still get single address pods?

This is not under our control. I mean , we are just rebooting the nodes in quick succession and at the end we just check the IP addresses of the above static pods. As i see the code , kubelet brings them up as soon as he is UP.

IMO the cloud provider really needs to figure out the IPs before kubelet starts. *OR* the node startup needs to block until both IP addresses are available so that the cloud provider and/or kubelet can read them.
Should we accept this as a bug?  Do we think we need to force some taint on new nodes that cloud-providers need to clear (obviously not compatible, but you get the idea)?

@thockin @aojea so i looked at this again. I believe https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/93898/ should fix this issue as well. i don't think we should place this behind a feature gate. We already update `.Status.HostIP` when the host IP changes. We just need to edit the release note of #93898 to describe the behavior and caveats.

Thoughts?

Interesting corner case from DanWinships test cases
```
			name: "CRI PodIPs override NodeAddresses",
			nodeAddresses: []v1.NodeAddress{
				{Type: v1.NodeInternalIP, Address: "10.0.0.1"},
				{Type: v1.NodeInternalIP, Address: "fd01::1234"},
			},
			criPodIPs: []string{"192.168.0.1"},
			podIPs: []v1.PodIP{
				{IP: "192.168.0.1"},
				{IP: "fd01::1234"},
```

CRIO and containerd doesn't send IPs for host network pods
https://github.com/cri-o/cri-o/blob/8d4d158935929800c4300b82eb4b5a83ded400f4/server/sandbox_network.go#L34-L36

https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/4921fb6b63e5476e54fb7e2cf93c3b505f1c09cb/pkg/cri/store/sandbox/sandbox.go#L40-L41

but they can.
I think that the discussion here is if override means removing IPs or just updating the ones that it sets leaving the others as is

I think override means "ignore CRI".

Do we think it is EVER correct for CRI to return host-net IPs?

> Do we think it is EVER correct for CRI to return host-net IPs?

I think we all agree that is a bad idea, but it seems that it is the way it was https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/106715#issuecomment-985943968

If *nothing* else we should specify what Kubernetes expects host-network pod IPs to be (order, number, type). I don't like leaving that an undefined wild-west.

And I think we should enforce that expectation. If there are corner cases that are currently possible that we break, I think a KEP should get written to implement that corner-case correctly.

Just for reference, the CRI IPs are obtained in kuberuntime in `GetPodStatus()`

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/571e067cddfbb0c2a3092ab9d3be3074043e3810/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go#L1064

and it seems they are stored in the PLEG cache

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/571e067cddfbb0c2a3092ab9d3be3074043e3810/pkg/kubelet/pleg/generic.go#L407-L419

This cache is used to `syncPod()` from the PodWorker

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/571e067cddfbb0c2a3092ab9d3be3074043e3810/pkg/kubelet/pod_workers.go#L904

and `generateAPIPodStatus()`

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/571e067cddfbb0c2a3092ab9d3be3074043e3810/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L1554

it seems there is no way to differentiate between:
- the CRI sets the IPs from CRI
- CRI does NOT return IPs, but Pod status IPs are updated incrementally,

> @danwinship what do you think?

I'm happy to declare that it was a bug that we ever let the CRI set hostNetwork pod IPs, but we should probably update the CRI docs to clarify this if so.
I've updated the commit with the CRI API change
Yes, this sounds good from the CRI API perspective :+1:
Do we also needto downgrade?  I feel like eventually we'll have to revisit this...
